paragraphs.text: The wounds caused by the fiery serpent are the poisonous enticements of the vices, which afflict the soul and bring about its spiritual death. The people were murmuring against the Lord. They were stricken by the serpents' bites. This provides an excellent instance of how one may recognize from the results of an external scourge what a great calamity a person might suffer inwardly by murmuring. In the raising up of the bronze serpent (when those who were stricken beheld it, they were cured) is prefigured our Redeemer's suffering on the cross, for only by faith in him is the kingdom of death and sin overcome.
paragraphs.author: Bede

paragraphs.text: The sins which drag down soul and body to destruction at the same time are appropriately represented by the serpents, not only because they were fiery and poisonous [and] artful at bringing about death but also because our first parents were led into sin by a serpent, and from being immortal they became mortal by sinning. The Lord is aptly made known by the bronze serpent, since he came in the likeness of sinful flesh.
paragraphs.author: Bede

paragraphs.text: Just as the bronze serpent had the likeness of a fiery serpent but had absolutely none of the strength of harmful poison in its members—rather by being lifted up it cured those who had been stricken by the [live] serpents—so the Redeemer of the human race did not merely clothe himself in sinful flesh but entered bodily into the likeness of sinful flesh, in order that by suffering death on the cross in [this likeness] he might free those who believed in him from all sin and even from death itself.
paragraphs.author: Bede

paragraphs.text: And that He might increase in them this fear, immediately, by the mouth of offence, the rod of His chastisement was revealed, and after the offence the Chastiser gave them no respite, because their servitude was not worthy of His longsuffering.
paragraphs.author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
paragraphs.work: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

paragraphs.text: Above their head the rod of justice hung continually, and immediately they committed sin they were chastened, and at the time of their offence they were beaten, and at the entrance of the path of their sins they forthwith received rebuke; for longsuffering teacheth the foolish servant contempt, and in order that that stupid nation, which in the manner of an evil-doing servant, sat in the house of God, might not [learn] contempt, the Chastiser took away longsuffering, especially when they went forth from Egypt.
paragraphs.author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
paragraphs.work: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

paragraphs.text: And we must also understand the object of that swift punishment in another way, and that there was not longsuffering as regardeth the correction of their sins; for God the Teacher took the people, like a child, from Egypt their nurse, that He might deliver unto them the doctrine of His knowledge, and might teach them the instruction of His wisdom. But the people, in their ignorance, when instruction had been delivered unto them, forgot it, and they never kept in remembrance the meditation of the commandments of God, and they were frequently punished with severity, so that, if it were only through fear of chastisement, they might lay hold upon the remembrance of instruction.
paragraphs.author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
paragraphs.work: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

paragraphs.text: The man who gathered sticks on the Sabbath day was stoned by all the congregation; and the earth opened and swallowed up others who were called by Moses, and who scorned him and came not; and fire went forth suddenly, and burnt up the bodies of others who thought lightly of his priestly office, and who sought honour for themselves; and others, who in the guise of paying honour, brought strange fire out of season, were burnt up by a tongue of fire which went forth from the tabernacle, and they perished; and others, because they asked for flesh and rejected the bread of angels, were tortured by the indigestion which came upon them; and others who went astray as concerning the calf, were pierced through by the swords of the Levites; and others, who were the cause of the revolt at the waters of trial were set apart for destruction; and others who murmured against the Lord perished by fiendish snakes; and likewise they all, because they strove against going into the land of promise, came to an end and were destroyed in the wilderness.
paragraphs.author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
paragraphs.work: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

paragraphs.text: To these offences, then, these punishments were united, and together with each act of wickedness a punishment straightway sprang up by its side, so that evil deeds might be suppressed by stripes, and sins by vengeance, and so that the people might be like a child who feareth the teacher who giveth him instruction, and that it might tremble before the Judge who would beat them like a wrongdoing slave.
paragraphs.author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
paragraphs.work: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

paragraphs.text: Many things were done in figure which were done in former times. For when he said that the fathers who were bitten by serpents in the desert could not be healed in any other way except that Moses hung up a brazen serpent, and when this was seen, those deadly bites and injurious effects of the poison were cured, he added: But these things were done in figure to instruct us (1 Corinthians 10:6). In the image, a bronze serpent was placed on a cross; because the true one to be crucified was announced to the human race, who would empty the venom of the devilish serpent, cursed in its image, but in truth, would erase all curses of the world.
paragraphs.author: Ambrose of Milan
paragraphs.work: Apology for the Prophet David, Chapter III

paragraphs.text: To be made whole of a serpent is a great sacrament. What is it to be made whole of a serpent by looking upon a serpent? It is to be made whole of death by believing in one dead. And nevertheless Moses feared and fled. What is it that Moses fled from that serpent? What, brethren, save that which we know to have been done in the gospel? Christ died, and the disciples feared and withdrew from that hope wherein they had been.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: The serpent struck Adam in paradise and killed him. [It also struck] Israel in the camp and annihilated them. "Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, the Son of Man will be lifted up." Just as those who looked with bodily eyes at the sign which Moses fastened on the cross lived bodily, so too those who look with spiritual eyes at the body of the Messiah nailed and suspended on the cross and believe in him will live [spiritually]. Thus it was revealed through this brazen [serpent], which by nature cannot suffer, that he who was to suffer on the cross is one who by nature cannot die.
paragraphs.author: Ephrem the Syrian

paragraphs.text: That brazen serpent was hung up as a remedy for the biting serpents, not as a type of him that suffered for us but as a contrast. It saved those that looked upon it, not because they believed it to live but because it was killed, and killed with it were the powers that were subject to it, being destroyed as it deserved. And what is the fitting epitaph for it from us? "O death, where is your sting? O grave, where is your victory?" You are overthrown by the cross. You are slain by him who is the giver of life. You are without breath, dead, without motion, even though you keep the form of a serpent lifted up high on a pole.
paragraphs.author: Gregory of Nazianzus

paragraphs.text: For tell me, was it not God who commanded by Moses that no image or likeness of anything which was in heaven above or which was on the earth should be made, and yet who caused the brazen serpent to be made by Moses in the wilderness, and set it up for a sign by which those bitten by serpents were saved? Yet is He free from unrighteousness. For by this, as I previously remarked, He proclaimed the mystery, by which He declared that He would break the power of the serpent which occasioned the transgression of Adam, and [would bring] to them that believe on Him [who was foreshadowed] by this sign, i.e., Him who was to be crucified, salvation from the fangs of the serpent, which are wicked deeds, idolatries, and other unrighteous acts.
paragraphs.author: Justin Martyr

paragraphs.text: The reading about the well and the song which Israel sang at the well has been recited to us from the book of Numbers — a reading which we see overflowing with mysteries in the usual measure, or rather perhaps even beyond the usual. For it says: "and from there, the well; this is the well of which the Lord said to Moses: Gather the people, and I will give them water to drink." But in these words the historical letter does not seem to me to possess much claim.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For what is it that the Lord so greatly commanded Moses to gather the people, that he might give them water to drink from the well? — as if indeed the people would not of their own accord come together at the well for the sake of drinking. Why, then, is it so emphatically commanded to the prophet, that by his own zeal and labor he should gather the people to draw the water of the well? Hence the cheapness of the letter sends us back to the preciousness of the spiritual understanding.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And therefore I think it fitting to gather the mysteries of wells also from other places of Scripture, so that from a comparison of many, if the present passage contains anything of obscurity, it may become clear. The Spirit of God therefore says through Solomon in Proverbs: "Drink waters from your own vessels and from the fountain of your own wells. And let not the waters be overpoured for you outside your own fountain" — although in other copies we have read: "and let the waters be poured out for you outside your own fountain." "Let your waters be for yourself alone, and let no stranger partake of them." Therefore each one of us has, as is designated in these words, a well within himself.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Nay, we say something even more: each one of us has not one well, but many wells, and not one vessel of water, but many vessels; for it did not say: "Drink waters from your vessel," but "from your vessels," and it did not say: "and from the fountain of your well," but "from the fountain of your wells." We read that the patriarchs too had wells: Abraham had them, Isaac also had them; and I think Jacob had them as well. And taking your beginning from these wells, run through all Scripture seeking wells, and come even to the Gospels, and there you will find the well above which our Savior sat resting after the labor of the journey — then, when the Samaritan woman came and wished to draw water from the well, the power of the well or of wells in the Scriptures is expounded, and a comparison of waters is made, where also the secrets of the divine mystery are laid open. For it is said that, if anyone drinks from these waters which that earthly well contained, he thirsts again; but whoever drinks from those which Jesus gives, there becomes in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. But in another place of the Gospel there is now spoken not of a fountain nor a well, but of something more. "He who believes in me," it says, "as the Scripture says, rivers of living water shall proceed from his belly." You see, then, that he who believes in him has within himself not only a well, but wells, and not only fountains, but rivers; and fountains and rivers not such as would console this mortal life, but such as would confer the eternal.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Therefore, according to those things which we set forth as written in Proverbs, where wells are named together with a fountain, the Word of God is to be understood as a well indeed, if it covers something of a deep mystery, but as a fountain, if it abounds and flows forth to the peoples.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But it must be inquired, not idly, how we can expound the plural number regarding the wells and the singular regarding the fountain, since in Proverbs Wisdom says: "Drink waters from the fountain of your wells." Let us see, then, of which wells it called the fountain one. I think that the knowledge of the unbegotten Father can be understood as one well, but the recognition of his only-begotten Son ought to be understood as another well. For the Son is other than the Father, and the Son is not the same as the Father, as he himself says in the Gospels: "It is another who bears witness of me, the Father." And again I think that the knowledge of the Holy Spirit can be seen as a third well. For he too is other than the Father and the Son, as it is likewise said of him in the Gospels: "The Father will send you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth." There is therefore this distinction of three persons in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, which is referred to the plural number of wells.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But of these wells there is one fountain; for the substance and nature of the Trinity is one. And in this way the distinction of the holy Scripture will be found not idle, which says: "from the fountain of your wells." But it marked the mystical utterances observantly, so that what was said in the plural should belong to the persons, and in the singular should fit the substance.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But those also can be seen as wells, of the knowledge of which he spoke who was filled with the wisdom of God: "For he gave me the true knowledge of the things that are, that I might know the substance of the world and the power of the elements, the beginning and end and middle of times, the changes of the vicissitudes and the alterations of the seasons, the cycles of the year and the positions of the stars, the natures of animals and the raging of beasts, the violences of spirits and the thoughts of men, the differences of plants and the powers of roots." You see how many wells there are in the knowledge of things?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: A well, for example, is the knowledge of plants, and perhaps the nature of each single plant has its own well. And likewise there is a well concerning the knowledge of animals, and perhaps each single species of animals has its own well. And again there is a well concerning the reckoning of times and their vicissitude and change. And since these individual things have a high and deep knowledge, they are rightly called wells figuratively.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And as long as the mystery of Christ was hidden from the ages and generations, the knowledge of these things was rightly called wells; but when, as Paul says, God revealed it to believers through his Spirit, all these become fountains and rivers, so that the knowledge of them is no longer held so in secret, but is brought forth to many and waters the believers and satisfies them. And therefore, I believe, the Savior was saying to his disciples that whoever believes in him and drinks the water of his teaching — there will be in him no longer a well nor a fountain, but rivers of living water.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For just as this one well, which is the Word of God, becomes innumerable wells and fountains and rivers, so also the soul of man, which is according to the image of God, can have within itself and produce from itself both wells and fountains and rivers. But in truth the wells which are in our soul need one who digs; for they must be cleansed, and everything that is earthly must be removed from them, so that those veins of rational senses which God implanted in it may produce pure and sincere streams. For as long as earth covers the veins of the waters and blocks the eye of the stream, the wave of pure liquid cannot flow forth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Finally, therefore it is written that the servants of Abraham were digging wells, and the Philistines were filling them and covering them with earth. But Isaac too, who had received the inheritance of his father, again dug wells and removed the earth of the Philistines, which they had thrown upon the waters through envy. But we have also observed this in Genesis, from which this history seems to be taken, that as long as Abraham was alive, the Philistines did not dare to fill the wells or throw earth on them; but when he departed from this life, then the Philistines prevailed and lay in wait against his wells. But afterward they are restored through Isaac and return to their state.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Moreover the servant of Abraham too, when he goes to betroth and bring back a wife for Isaac, found Rebecca at the wells — she who is interpreted as "patience": she is made the wife of Isaac nowhere else but at the wells. Similarly Jacob too, when he came to Mesopotamia having the command of his father not to take a wife of foreign race or of alien blood, himself also found Rachel at the wells. And Moses found Zipporah at the wells.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: If, then, you have understood what and of what sort are the wives of the saints, you too, if you wish to take patience to yourself in marriage, or wisdom, or whatever those virtues of the soul are, and to say what was said of wisdom: "Her I sought to bring to myself as a wife" — be frequent, be assiduous around those wells, and there you will find a spouse of this kind. For at the living waters, that is, at the streams of the living word, it is certain that all the virtues of the soul dwell. There are therefore many wells, which we have said to be within the soul. And there are very many others, which are understood in each single word and sense of the Scriptures.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Yet more eminent than the rest and outstanding is this well, of which in the present passage Scripture says that it was dug not by any common men whatsoever, but by princes, and by those still more sublime than these, whom it called kings; on account of which also a hymn is sung to God at this same well. And therefore it is written: "Go," it says, "to the well. This is the well of which the Lord said to Moses: Gather the people, and I will give them water from the well, says the Lord." Moses is commanded to gather the people, that it may come together to the well and drink water; and we have often shown that Moses ought to be taken as the Law. It is therefore the Law of God which calls you together, that you may come to the well. What well, except that one of which we spoke above — Jesus Christ the Son of God, subsisting indeed in his own substance, yet named with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the one fountain of the Godhead?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: To this well, then, that is, to faith in Christ, the Law calls us together. For he himself says: "Moses wrote of me." For what does it call us together? That we may drink the waters and sing to it a song, that is, that we may believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: "Initiate the well for it," it says. This is the sense: set, it says, the well as the beginning of all things, just as the Apostle also says that "he is the beginning, and the firstborn of every creature, and in him all things were created." Initiate the well for it, therefore — that is, confess the well to be the beginning of all things. But it can also be understood in this way, that the words seem to be directed from the person of Moses, exhorting the people and saying: Give a beginning to your heart, that it may begin to understand what the well is, from which the spiritual waters are to be drawn and by which the people of believers is to be refreshed.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Initiate this well, therefore, for it, that is, for Israel, so that whoever sees God with the heart may be able to draw the mystical sense from the depths. That Moses, that is the Law, should gather us to this well does not seem to be said in vain. For it can happen that someone may seem to come to this well, but unless he is gathered through Moses, he is not accepted by God. Marcion seems to himself to have come to this well, and Basilides and Valentinus, but because they did not come through Moses nor receive the Law and the prophets, they cannot praise the Lord God from the fountains of Israel.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Therefore those who are of this kind do not come to the well which the princes dug and the kings hewed out. But do you wish me to show you from the Scriptures to what wells these men come? There is a certain salt valley, in which valley are wells of bitumen; every heresy therefore and every sin is in a valley, and in a salt valley. For sin and iniquity does not ascend upward, but always descends to the lowest and infernal places. Every heretical understanding, therefore, and every act of sin is both set in a valley and salt and bitter.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For what sweet, what pleasant thing can sin have? But it has something even more. For if you come to a heretical opinion, if you come to the bitterness of sin, you have come to the wells of bitumen. Bitumen is food and nourishment for fire. If therefore you too taste water from these wells, if you take up a heretical understanding, if you receive the bitterness of sin, you will prepare within yourself the kindling of fire and the burnings of Gehenna.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And therefore to those who are unwilling to drink water from that well which the princes dig and the kings, but from these which are in the valley of sin and feed the fuel of fire, it is said: "Walk in the light of your fire and of the flame which you have kindled for yourselves." What, then, is sung at this well? "Initiate the well for it," it says; "the princes dug it, the kings hewed it out." The princes and the kings can indeed seem to be the same; but if it is necessary to distinguish them, let us understand the princes as the prophets.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For they placed the meaning and prophecy concerning Christ dug down and submerged in the depth of the letter, and therefore one of them said: "Unless you hear in secret, your soul will weep." And likewise another prophet says to the Lord: "How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!" These, then, are the princes who dug this well, but the kings are those who hewed it out. That it said "hewed out" (excuderunt) is said from "hammering out" (excudere), not from "cutting away" (excidere); for that is said to be "hammered out" which is either cut or shaped in stone.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The princes therefore, as being somewhat inferior, are said to dig the well, that is, as it were to sink a certain depth in the softness of the earth. But these, whom it calls kings, as being stronger and more eminent, penetrate not only the depth of the earth but also the hardness of the rock, that they may be able to reach the deeper waters and, if it may be said, search out in it the very veins of the abyss, knowing that the judgments of God are a great abyss. These kings, then, who can search out things so deep and so hidden of the well, we may rightly call the Apostles, one of whom said: "But to us God has revealed it through the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God." Because, therefore, through the Spirit they too can search out the deep things of God and penetrate the high and deep mysteries of the well, they are for that reason said to be kings, who hewed out this well even in the rock and penetrated the hard and difficult secrets of knowledge. That the Apostles too can be called kings, I think can easily be proved from this, which is said of all believers: "But you are a royal race, a great priesthood, a holy nation." If, then, they call kings those who believed through their word, how much more are they themselves to be held as kings, who make kings?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But from this too it is easily gathered: for if kings are named from ruling, then certainly all who rule the churches of God will rightly be called kings, but much more rightly those who by their words and writings rule even those very men by whom the churches are ruled. And on account of this the Lord is rightly called King of kings; for unless these and the rest who imitate them are kings, he will not appear as King of kings.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But the Apostle Paul himself too, writing to the Corinthians and rebuking them as it were with a certain irony, says: "Without us you reign; and would that you did reign, that we too might reign with you." In which he certainly declares that the Corinthians ought to be kings and that he himself wishes to reign with them, but he reproaches their elation over an honor not yet assumed according to merit.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: All these princes, then, dig this well, and the kings of the nations hew it out; for the Apostles are especially the kings of the nations, who gathered the nations to the obedience of faith and laid open the knowledge of Christ to all — in whom are the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God hidden — going around the circle of the earth according to the command of the Lord and fulfilling what was commanded, that they should teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; and by these things they hewed out, that is, laid open the knowledge of the well and brought it into the knowledge of all the nations.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But these things too which we now have in hand, which have been recited to us, are a well, and all the scripture of the Law and the prophets together; the Evangelical and Apostolic scripture also, all together, is one well, which they cannot dig or hew out unless they are found to be kings and princes. For truly they are to be held kings, truly princes, who can remove the earth from this well and take away the surface of the letter and from the inner rock, where Christ is, bring forth the spiritual senses like living water.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: This, therefore, it is fitting that those alone do who are either kings or princes; called kings from this, that they have driven out the reign of sin from their body and have prepared the reign of righteousness in their members. For it is fitting that he teach others who has first done the very things which he teaches.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For thus it is written: "Whoever shall do and shall so teach men, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." But to be great in the kingdom, this is to be a king. "The kings of the nations hewed it out," it says — in their kingdom, while they ruled over them. For in very truth they cannot dig this well nor open the hidden veins of living water, unless they have first held dominion over the barbarous nations. For everything whatsoever that was wild in them in their acts, whatever was barbarous in their conduct — if they have tamed it and subjected it to the royal understanding and held dominion over it, so that henceforth they act not like the heathen but lawfully — these are truly kings, probing the depths of the well and searching out the hidden and mystical things of the Word of God.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: After these things "they set out," he says, "from the well to Mattanah, and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth, and from Bamoth to the grove which is in the field of Moab, from the top of the hewn mountain that looks toward the face of the desert." These names, which appear to be the designations of places, seem — from their significations, which they denote in their own tongue — to display the sequence of things rather mystical rather than merely a naming of places.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: "For having set out," he says, "from the well they come to Mattanah." For Mattanah is interpreted "their gifts." You see, then, that if anyone has drunk from this well which the kings and princes dug, he straightway advances to this, that he has gifts to offer to God. But what is it that a person offers to God? This very thing which is written in the law: "my gifts, my offerings." From those things, therefore, which God has given, human beings nonetheless make offerings to God. What did God give to man? Knowledge of himself. What does man offer to God? His faith and his affection.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: This is what God seeks from man. And indeed it is thus written: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, and walk in his ways, and love him, and keep all his commandments, and serve the Lord your God with your whole heart and with your whole soul?" These are the gifts, these the offerings which ought to be given to the Lord. And we give to the Lord these gifts of our heart after we have come to know him and have drunk from the depth of his well the knowledge of his goodness.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Observe, however, how the prophet said: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you?" Let these words put to shame those who deny that it lies within man's choice that he be saved. For how would God ask of man, unless man had within his own power that which he ought to offer to God who asks? There are, then, things which are given by God, and there are things which are furnished by man. For example, it lay within the man to make one mina into ten minas, or one mina into five minas; but it was from God that the man had a mina from which he could make ten minas.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But when he offered from himself the ten minas, he received in turn from God no longer money, but power and rule over ten cities. Again God asks of Abraham that he offer to him his son Isaac upon a mountain, whichever one he should show him. Abraham offered his only-begotten undaunted, laid him upon the altar, drew the knife to slay him — he is at once restrained, and a ram is given to him for a victim in place of his son. You see, then, that the things which we offer to God remain ours, but we are asked for them to this end, that in them our affection toward God and our faith may be tested.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: So much for what we said, that the children of Israel set out from the well and came to Mattanah, which is interpreted "their gifts." And from Mattanah we come to Nahaliel, which is interpreted "from God." What is "from God"? After we have offered the things that are from ourselves, we come to this, that we may attain the things that are from God. For when we have offered to him our faith and our affection, then he too bestows upon us the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, of which the Apostle says: "But all things are from God." And from Nahaliel we come to Bamoth, which is interpreted "the coming of death." What coming of death do we understand here, except that by which we die together with Christ, so that we may also live together with him, and by which we ought to mortify our members which are upon the earth, and again: "for we are buried together with him through baptism into death"?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: If anyone, then, holds to the order of this saving way, he ought to journey through each of these things which we have recalled, and to come after many stages to this place, which we said signifies the coming of death. But, as we are taught from the Scriptures, there is a certain death that is an enemy of Christ, and a certain death that is his friend.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: He does not, therefore, speak of that death that is the enemy of Christ, of which it is said: "the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed," which is the devil, but of this death, by which we die together with him, so that we may also live together with him — according to which death God says: "I will kill and I will make alive." For he kills, that we may die together with Christ, and he makes alive, that we may live together with him. It is therefore to be wished by us that we come to Bamoth and most readily receive the coming of this blessed death, so that we may deserve also to be made alive with Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: "And from Bamoth," he says, "to the grove which is in the field of Moab, from the top of the hewn mountain that looks toward the desert." If we walk by this journey, which the reasoning of our explanation has asserted consists not so much of the names of places as of the advances of the soul, after all these things we come to the grove, or, as it stands in other copies, to Janah, which is interpreted "the ascent" or "the top of the mountain." Through these things, therefore, one arrives either at that most renowned grove of the divine paradise and the pleasant delights of the ancient habitation, or certainly at the summit of perfection and the height of blessedness, so that you too may be able to say that "he raised us up together with him, and made us sit in the heavenly places in Christ." Do you see how far one arrives from the well? Do you see by what stations, or rather by what advances, the soul's journey to heaven is prepared? If you examine these things diligently, you yourself, discerning within your own self your daily advances, will perceive in what places you are and how near you are held to be to the kingdom of heaven; just as also that man of whom the Lord said that "you are not far from the kingdom of God."
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: After this there follows yet another narrative. For it says: "And Moses sent" — or, as it stands in some copies, "And Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites with words of peace, saying: We will pass through your land; by the road we will pass; we will not turn aside either into a field or into a vineyard. We will not drink water from your well; we will go by the royal road, until we pass your borders. And Sihon did not grant that Israel should pass through his borders; and Sihon gathered all his people, and went out to make war against Israel in the desert; and he came to Jahaz, and joined battle with Israel.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And Israel struck him down with the slaughter of the sword, and they took possession of his land." The narrative indeed is plain, but let us beseech the Lord that we may be able to discern something worthy in its inner meanings. Sihon has a double interpretation, either "unfruitful tree" or "lifted up." Israel therefore sends messengers to Sihon: it sends to the unfruitful tree, it sends to the one lifted up and proud.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Now this Sihon is king of the Amorites, who themselves are interpreted as "those bringing into bitterness" or "speaking." Moses therefore sends to Sihon king of the Amorites with words of peace, saying: "We will pass through your land." If, according to the spiritual understanding, we say that Sihon the king holds the figure of the devil, because he himself is lifted up and unfruitful, I think you ought not to wonder that I have called him a king, since you hear even our very Lord and Savior in the Gospels saying concerning him: "Behold, now comes the prince of this world, and in me he will find nothing," and again: "Behold, now the prince of this world shall be cast out." If therefore he is called in the Gospels the prince of the whole world, it ought not to seem absurd if he is compared to Sihon king of the Amorites, or even to any other kings of the nations whatsoever.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But he is called prince of the world not because he created the world, but because there are many sinners in this world. And because he himself is the prince of sin, therefore he has also been called the prince of the world — namely, among those who, not yet abandoning the world, are converted to the Father.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For it is according to this that that also is said: "the whole world is set in wickedness." For what does it profit us to say that our prince is Christ, if by our deeds and works we are convicted that the devil holds the princedom in us? Or is it not plain under which prince the unchaste, the incestuous, the unjust man acts? Can a man of this sort say that, set under Christ, he does these things, even if he seems to be reckoned under the name of Christ? In whom Christ bears the princedom, there no uncleanness, no iniquity is admitted, nor can unjust desire have any place.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: According to this manner, then, rightly will Christ be called the prince of the virtues, and the devil of malice and of all iniquity.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Israel therefore sends messengers to the king of the Amorites, the king of those who provoke into bitterness, the unfruitful king, the proud king. In what way will the devil be shown to be proud, in what way lifted up? He it is who said: "By my strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the borders of the nations, and I will plunder their might; and I will shake the cities which are inhabited, and the whole circle of the earth I will take in my hand like a nest." And again this lifted-up and proud one says: "I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, I will sit upon a lofty mountain above the high mountains which are toward the north, I will ascend above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High." Do you still ask whether he himself is lifted up and proud?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Nay rather, both he himself is proud and lifted up, and that one who is, as it were, his only-begotten, of whom it is written that "he shall be exalted above everything that is called God or that is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself off as though he were God." Everyone therefore who is lifted up and proud is either a son of this lifted-up one, or a disciple and imitator.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And for this reason the Apostle says concerning a certain one: "lest perhaps, being lifted up, he fall into the judgment of the devil," showing by this that everyone who is lifted up will be condemned by a like judgment, as the devil is. We therefore are those who wish to pass through this world, that we may be able to arrive at the holy land, which has been promised to the saints; and we send with words of peace to Sihon, promising that we will not dwell in his land nor tarry with him, but only pass through and walk by the royal road, nor turn aside anywhere, neither into a field nor into a vineyard, but that we will not even drink water from his well. Let us see, then, when we promised these things, when we announced these words to the devil.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Let each of the faithful call to mind, when he first came to the waters of baptism, when he received the first seals of the faith and approached the fountain of salvation, what words he then used there and what he announced to the devil: that he would not make use of his pomps, nor of his works, nor at all yield to any of his services and pleasures.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And this is what is foreshadowed in these words of the law, that Israel would not turn aside either into his field or into his vineyard, but that it promises it will not drink water even from his well. For no longer will the faithful one take the cup of diabolical instruction, not of astrology, not of magic, not at all of any teaching which teaches anything against the piety of God. For he has his own fountains, and Israel drinks from the fountains, drinks from the fountains of salvation; he does not drink water from the well of Sihon, nor, forsaking the fountain of living water, does he gather for himself broken cisterns.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But he also professes that he will walk by the royal road. What is the royal road? That one, without doubt, which says: "I am the way and the truth and the life." And rightly royal; for it is he of whom the prophet says: "God, give your judgment to the king." By the royal road, therefore, one must walk, nor turn aside anywhere, neither into his field nor into his vineyard — that is, the mind of the faithful ought no longer to turn aside either to diabolical works or to diabolical senses. In what way, then, do we wish to pass through the borders of the Amorites with peace?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The Amorites can be taken as the portion of the unbelievers who are in this world; but these are interpreted, as we said above, either as "those bringing into bitterness" or "speaking." And in what way indeed the unbelievers and the incredulous bring God into bitterness needs no exposition; but what he says, "speaking," can be drawn to that part, that all who are unbelieving and act under the devil as prince know only how to speak, but they speak empty things. For example, as their poets, as the astrologers, as some even of the philosophers, who speak things empty and vain. But the kingdom of the faithful, which is from God, is not in speech, but in power.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: We therefore wish to pass through the world peacefully, but this very thing rather incites the prince of the world, that we say we are unwilling to remain with him nor to tarry nor to wish to touch anything of his; from that he is the more exasperated, from that he is provoked and grows angry and stirs up persecutions against us, rouses dangers, threatens torments. And therefore it says: "Sihon," it says, "gathered all his people, and went out to fight against Israel." Who is all the people of Sihon, whom he stirs up against Israel? The princes and judges of the world and all the ministers of wickedness, who always assail and persecute the people of God. But what does Israel do? "It came," it says, "to Jahaz." Jahaz is interpreted "the fulfilling of the commandment." If therefore we too come to this place, that is, to the fulfilling of the commandments, even if that lifted-up and proud Sihon, the devil, come against us with his whole army and fight against us, if he stir up all his demons against us, we overcome him, if we fulfill the commandments of God. For to fulfill the commandments is to overcome the devil and his whole army. And then there will be fulfilled in us the prayer of the Apostle, in which he says: "But God will crush Satan under your feet speedily," and that which the Lord says: "Behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you." For all these things will be able to do us no harm, if we come to Jahaz, that is, if we keep the commandments and precepts of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Yesterday we spoke of how Sihon, king of the Amorites, who is the lofty one and the barren tree, having engaged with Israel was defeated; concerning whom Scripture also says pointedly that he fell "by the slaughter of the sword" or, as we read elsewhere, "by the mouth of the sword." But if you wish to know more carefully by what sword this barren and lofty one, "like the cedar of Lebanon," fell, let us learn from the Apostle Paul, who says: "For the word of God is living and effective and more piercing than any sword," and again in another place: "and the sword," he says, "of the spirit, which is the word of God." By the slaughter of this sword, then, fell the spiritual Sihon, who is the devil.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: After these things it is added: "and the sons of Israel," he says, "had dominion over all his land." All this earthly region indeed is called the land of Sihon, but Christ and his Church have dominion over all the land of Sihon. "And they had dominion from Arnon as far as Jabbok." Arnon and Jabbok were cities of the kingdom of Sihon, but the beginning of his kingdom was Arnon and the end was Jabbok, and therefore it is said that "they had dominion from Arnon as far as Jabbok." Now Arnon is interpreted "their curses"; the beginning, therefore, of the kingdom of this lofty and barren Sihon is curses.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But the end is Jabbok, which is interpreted "wrestling"; for it is necessary that everyone who wishes to go out from the kingdom of the devil and to escape his borders should find wrestling, and that contests be stirred up against him by his ministers and satellites. But if he has wrestled and conquered, then Jabbok will no longer be a city of Sihon, but will be a city of Israel. This is doubtless what we read also concerning the patriarch Jacob, since, when he had come to a certain place, a wrestling was prepared for him, and there, when he had wrestled the whole night and had prevailed and grown strong before God, his name was called Israel.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: "And Israel took," he says, "all these cities; and Israel dwelt in all the cities of the Amorites." This Israel, who is Israel in Christ, who is Israel not in the flesh, nor a Jew in what is manifest, he himself dwells in all the cities of the Amorites when in all the world the churches of Christ are being propagated.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But each one of us also was formerly a city of King Sihon, the lofty king; for there reigned in us folly, pride, impiety, and all the things that are on the devil's side; but when the strong one was overcome and vanquished and his vessels plundered, we were made cities of Israel and the inheritance of the saints—if indeed that power which formerly ruled over us has been utterly cut off in us, and the barren tree has been cut down, and the lofty king has been cast down, and we are under that king who says: "learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart." After these things he now enumerates one by one the cities of the proud and barren king, and says: "in Heshbon and in all its neighboring places." What is this, that he named Heshbon as the chief city of the kingdom of Sihon? Heshbon is interpreted "thoughts." Rightly, then, does the greatest part of the diabolical kingdom and the greater part of its power reign in thoughts; for so the Lord also said: "out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies; and these are the things that defile a man." And therefore this city is necessarily set ablaze and consumed by fire. By what fire? Surely by that of which the Savior says: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it be kindled!"
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But after a few words it is reported concerning that very city: "For this reason," he says, "the riddlers shall say: come into Heshbon, that the city of Sihon may be built and constructed; for fire went forth from Heshbon and a flame from the city of Sihon, and it devoured as far as Moab." Sihon, as we said, was the king, whose city was Heshbon. Thus, then, the order of the words is to be understood, that these riddlers say: come, that Heshbon, which was the city of Sihon, may be built and constructed. But let us now inquire who these riddlers are. A riddle is a figured saying; riddlers therefore are those who speak figuratively.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And who else is there who has spoken in figures except the law and the prophets? For hear how David says: "I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter propositions from the beginning." But Isaiah too, that the things he wrote are riddles, declares in this manner: "and the words of this book shall be," he says, "like the words of a sealed book; which if they give into the hands of a man who does not know letters and say to him: read, he will say: I do not know letters. But if they give it to one who knows letters, he will say: I cannot read, for it is sealed." Now the book is called sealed for the reason that it is entangled with figures and wrapped up in riddles.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: These riddlers, then, say: come into Heshbon, that it may be built. That first Heshbon fell, or rather was overturned and burned; another is to be rebuilt. But how this is done, let us show by taking up an example. If you see a Gentile placed in the disgrace of life and in the error of religion, do not hesitate to say of him that here is the city of Heshbon in the kingdom of King Sihon; for the barren and lofty king reigns in his thoughts.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: If Israel—that is, a son of the Church—approaches this man and applies the darts of the word of God and unsheathes against him the sword of the spirit, and destroys in him all the fortifications of Gentile teachings and burns up the loftinesses of his arguments with the fire of truth, say of this man that the city of Heshbon of Sihon is overthrown. But this man, in whom the teachings of the Gentiles are overthrown, is not straightway left deserted and abandoned.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For it is not the discipline of the sons of Israel to leave in ruins the cities that they have destroyed; but when they have undermined and overturned in a man his evil thoughts and impious sentiments, they build again in the heart of him whom they have destroyed good thoughts, pious sentiments; they will implant the doctrine of truth, they will hand on the rite of religion, they will teach the order of living, honesty of morals, they will show the statutes of observance. And then these riddlers will truly say to one another in turn: come and let us build Heshbon, which was the city of Sihon.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For they themselves too—that is, the sons of the Church—because they understand the figures of the law and the riddles spiritually, are called riddlers. This is what Jeremiah also designates by a no less figurative saying, where it is said to him by the Lord: "behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have appointed you this day over the nations and kingdoms, to root up and to overturn and to rebuild and to replant." What does he root up and what does he overturn? The city of Heshbon, which was Sihon's. What does he root up in it and what does he overturn? Impious and impure thoughts. What does he rebuild in it and what does he replant?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Pious and chaste thoughts, so that Heshbon may be made a city not of the Amorites, but of the sons of Israel.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if we wish to pursue each point, we shall be shut out from the discussion of those things which were read to us concerning Balaam; the reading of which is of such difficulty that we can scarcely arrive at explaining the account and sequence of the history itself. How great, then, will now be our difficulty in explaining the spiritual senses, if the very surface of the letter is wrapped in such great difficulties?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But although desire snatches us toward discussing the things which are more obscure, nevertheless these things also, which are reported in between, are not to be entirely passed over. For after the sons of Israel had obtained the cities of the Amorites, they went up also by the way which leads into Bashan, where Og, king of Bashan, was; but to this one they neither deign to send envoys nor to ask of him that they may pass through his land, but immediately they clash with him and overcome both him and his people. Let us see, then, what Bashan is. Bashan is interpreted "baseness"; rightly, then, are neither envoys sent to that nation nor is passage through its land requested.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For there ought to be for us no passage, no approach to baseness, but from the very beginning at once it must be assaulted and in every way guarded against. Now Og, who is said to be king of Bashan, is interpreted "enclosure." This can hold the figure of all carnal and material things, by love and desire of which the soul, being held fast, is shut out and separated from God. Against these, therefore, war is commanded to be waged in such a way that "you shall not leave," he says, "of him one living"; for none must be left by the sons of Israel living in the kingdom of baseness and disgrace.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But it befits Israelite virtue to cut down and cut away base things and to rebuild in the soul whatever is pious and to plant honorable and religious things. Concerning the kingdom of Sihon it is not written that no living one be left, nor concerning the kingdom of Moab; for perhaps we have need of some of them, and we require certain of them for the contests and exercises of this life; otherwise we should have had to go out of this world. Of Bashan, however—that is, of baseness—we have need of none whatsoever; let us leave nothing of it; all things must be cut down, all the works of baseness must be overturned; for in nothing can that which is base be honorable.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
